questions.q: what do we learn about Hannibal from these opening words?

questions.q: explain in your own words what Nepos thinks might have happened.

questions.q: how does Nepos emphasise Hannibal’s determination in these lines?

questions.q: explain in your own words what Nepos says about Philip.

questions.q: what part of the world does Nepos mean by this?

questions.q: explain in your own words how Hannibal began his conversation with the king.

questions.q: why do you think Nepos uses this title for the god?

questions.q: what impression of the young Hannibal do we get, and how does Nepos create it?

questions.q: how does Nepos make Hamilcar’s reply forceful?

questions.q: how does Nepos make the taking of the oath solemn and private?

ad aram: at the altar, a sacred place
where the sacrifice had begun (sacrificare instituerat)

questions.lemma: numquam me in amicitia cum Romanis fore

be a friend of the Romans / on friendly terms with Rome

questions.q: how does Hannibal stress his faithfulness to the oath?
points: id ego iusiurandum: the oath is placed first, with the emphatic pronoun ego
patri datum: it was given to his father, so it is a family duty
usque ad hanc aetatem: he has kept it from boyhood to old age
ita conservavi: he has kept it so completely
questions.guidance: Accept any three. Each point must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: how does Hannibal show confidence in his own value?
points: te ipsum frustraberis: he bluntly tells a king that he would only fool himself
he says Antiochus must put him in command of the war
principem is the last word of his speech: a claim to leadership
the contrast with the earlier advice to hide peace plans shows he is useful only for war against Rome

questions.q: what does Nepos mean by these words, and why does he add them?
points: ‘at the age we mentioned’: when Hannibal was nine
qua diximus: Nepos steps back into his own narrative after Hannibal’s speech
it rounds off the story (ring structure) and returns to the start of his career

questions.q: describe in detail how Hannibal came to swear his oath.
points: while the sacrifice was being carried out
Hamilcar asked if he wanted to go with him to the camp
Hannibal gladly accepted
he begged his father not to hesitate to take him
Hamilcar agreed, if Hannibal gave him the pledge he asked for
he led him to the altar
everyone else was sent away
Hannibal held the altar
he swore that he would never be a friend of the Romans

questions.q: why was Spain so important to Carthage at this time?
points: Carthage had lost Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica to Rome after the First Punic War
Spain had silver mines
and manpower
it gave Carthage the resources for a second war

questions.q: how does Nepos stress that Hannibal’s appointment was legitimate?
points: the army itself gave him supreme command (exercitus … ad eum detulit)
publice comprobatum est: it was officially approved by the state
detulit … delatum: the same verb links the soldiers’ choice to the city’s approval
so the command was given to him, with no hint that he seized it by force

questions.q: what happened after Hamilcar’s death?
points: Hasdrubal took over as commander
Hannibal was put in charge of all the cavalry

questions.lemma: minor quinque et viginti annis natus
questions.q: why do you think Nepos gives Hannibal’s age so precisely here?
points: it spells out how young he was: not yet twenty-five
the reader is struck that so young a man commanded a whole army
it marks him out as exceptional from the very start

questions.q: what did Hannibal achieve after he became commander?
points: he was not yet twenty-five
within the next three years
he conquered all the peoples of Spain
he took Saguntum by force
a city allied to Rome
he raised three very large armies
he sent one to Africa
he left one in Spain with his brother Hasdrubal
he led the third into Italy himself

questions.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s achievements in Spain seem astonishing?
points: hyperbole omnes gentes Hispaniae: every people of Spain
proximo triennio: all within three years
asyndeton: three achievements follow with no connecting words, giving rapid, relentless activity
vi expugnavit: Saguntum taken by force
superlative maximos: the armies were very large
questions.guidance: Accept any three. Each point must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what later became of this Hasdrubal?
points: he held Spain for Carthage until 208 BC
he led an army into Italy to reinforce Hannibal
he was defeated and killed at the Metaurus (207 BC)

questions.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s own army stand out?
points: tricolon: the three armies are dealt out in three balanced clauses (unum … alterum … tertium)
the climax is the third army, the one he leads himself (secum duxit)
its destination, in Italiam, is the most important

questions.q: how does Nepos emphasise Hannibal’s success on the march?
points: quacumque: wherever he went
cum omnibus incolis: he fought every people he met
emphatic negative neminem nisi victum: no exceptions, everyone was beaten
short clauses / asyndeton give a sense of speed
questions.guidance: Accept any three. Each point must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what legend lies behind this reference?
points: Hercules was said to have crossed the Alps
on his way back from Spain
with the cattle of Geryon
the Graian Alps were linked with his name

questions.lemma: ad Alpes posteaquam … vix poterat repere
questions.q: describe Hannibal’s crossing of the Alps.
points: the Alps separate Italy from Gaul
no one had crossed them with an army before him
except the Greek Hercules
so the pass is still called the Graian Pass
he cut down the Alpine tribes
who tried to stop him crossing
he opened up the terrain
he built roads
a fully laden elephant could now go
where before a single unarmed man could barely crawl

questions.q: explain in your own words what had already happened at the Rhone.
points: Hannibal had already fought a battle against Scipio
Scipio was consul at the time
Hannibal had driven him back / defeated him

questions.lemma: cum hoc eodem … tertio idem Scipio
questions.q: how does Nepos emphasise that Hannibal kept beating the same Roman commander?
points: hoc eodem: ‘this same man’ stresses that it is the same commander again
idem Scipio repeats the point
tertio: Nepos counts the defeats
the historic presents decernit … dimittit make the second defeat vivid
sauciumque … ac fugatum: a humiliating picture of a consul both wounded and running
questions.guidance: Accept any three; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: how does Nepos make this victory sound swift and complete?
points: asyndeton: two short clauses with no connecting word
the battle is over as soon as it begins
utrosque: both consuls together are beaten
profligavit: a strong word, ‘crushed’
questions.guidance: Accept any two; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what impression of Hannibal does Nepos create here, and how?
points: he seems human / vulnerable, a man who suffers
adeo gravi morbo: the illness is very severe
numquam: the harm to his eye is permanent
the suffering comes in the middle of his victories, which makes them more remarkable

questions.q: what happened to Flaminius?
points: he was a consul
at Lake Trasimene
he was surrounded / caught in an ambush
he was killed
together with his army

questions.q: what happened at this place?
points: (in 217 BC) Hannibal trapped Flaminius’ army
in mist between the hills and the lake shore
Flaminius was killed
with about 15,000 Romans

questions.q: who were these men?
points: the two consuls (of 216 BC) who commanded against Hannibal at Cannae

questions.q: what happened to Hannibal between the Rhone and his march into Etruria?
points: he fought Scipio at the Rhone and drove him back
he fought the same man again at Clastidium on the Po
Scipio was left wounded and routed
Scipio came against him a third time at the Trebia
with his colleague Tiberius Longus
Hannibal crushed them both
he crossed the Apennines through the land of the Ligurians
he caught a severe disease of the eyes
he never again had the full use of his right eye

questions.q: how does Nepos show the scale of Rome’s losses?
points: climax: the list rises from a consul to a group of ex-consuls
aliquot praeterea consulares: several former consuls died as well
Cn. Servilium Geminum: naming one victim makes the loss precise
qui superiore anno fuerat consul: he had been consul only a year before, which makes it personal for Roman readers
questions.guidance: Accept any three; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: explain in your own words what Hannibal did after the battle.
points: he marched on Rome
no one tried to stop him
he stayed for some time
in the hills close to the city

questions.lemma: in propinquis urbi montibus moratus est
questions.q: why might Roman readers find this detail alarming?
points: Hannibal was camped within sight of Rome
propinquis urbi stresses how close he was
moratus est (‘he lingered’) hints at a missed chance to attack
after nullo resistente, nothing stood between him and the city

questions.q: why was this city important to Hannibal at this time?
points: the richest city of Campania went over to him after Cannae
it served as his base

questions.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s escape seem impressive?
points: clausus: he appears trapped
locorum angustiis: the narrow ground leaves no way out
noctu: he gets a whole army out in the dark
sine ullo detrimento: ullo stresses that not a single man was lost
the superlative callidissimo praises the very man he fools
questions.guidance: Accept any three; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.lemma: quo repentino visu … nemo sit ausus
questions.q: how does Nepos emphasise the Romans’ fear?
points: repentino: the shock of the sudden sight
tantum terrorem: the size of the terror, with alliteration of t
the result clause ut … nemo sit ausus shows its effect
nemo: not one man dared
a whole Roman army stays behind its wall (extra vallum)
questions.guidance: Accept any three; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: explain how Hannibal defeated Minucius.
points: Minucius was Master of Horse
with power equal to the dictator’s
Hannibal lured him into battle
by a trick
and routed him

questions.q: what happened to Gracchus and Marcellus?
points: Gracchus was consul for the second time
he was lured into an ambush in Lucania
Hannibal destroyed him without being there himself
Marcellus had been consul five times
he was killed near Venusia
in the same way (by an ambush)

questions.q: who was Marcellus?
points: he captured Syracuse
he was called the Sword of Rome
he had been consul five times
he died in an ambush near Venusia (in 208 BC)

questions.q: how does Nepos emphasise Hannibal’s greatness?
points: hoc unum … satis: a single fact is enough to prove it
quantus ille fuerit: ille gives a grand, admiring tone
quamdiu in Italia fuit: the claim covers his whole time in Italy
anaphora of nemo … nemo drives the point home
post Cannensem pugnam: after Cannae no one even dared to camp near him
questions.guidance: Accept any three; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: describe how Hannibal outwitted Fabius and then Minucius.
points: he was trapped by the narrowness of the ground
he got his army out at night
without any loss
he tied bundles of twigs to the horns of young cattle
he set them alight
he sent many of the cattle scattering
the sudden sight terrified the Romans
no one dared to go outside the rampart
not many days later he lured Minucius (Master of Horse) into battle by a trick and routed him

questions.q: explain in your own words why Hannibal left Italy.
points: he was called home
to defend his own country
he left still unbeaten

questions.q: why do you think Nepos makes this the first word of the chapter?
points: it stresses that Hannibal left Italy unbeaten
so his record in Italy stands whatever happens at Zama
it secures the reader’s admiration before the defeat is told

questions.lemma: primo apud Rhodanum, iterum apud Padum, tertio apud Trebiam
questions.q: how does Nepos remind the reader of Hannibal’s earlier successes against this family?
points: tricolon of three battles
the numbered stages primo … iterum … tertio
repetition of apud with each place
the father’s defeats are recalled just as the son steps forward
questions.guidance: Accept any two; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what impression of Hannibal’s motives does Nepos give, and how?
points: exhaustis … patriae facultatibus: Carthage’s weakness is given as the reason for seeking peace
so the blame for the defeat is moved away from Hannibal
impraesentiarum: the peace is only for the time being
quo valentior postea congrederetur: he is still planning the next war
even his peace offer is a military tactic

questions.q: why do you think Nepos describes the outcome of Zama so briefly?
points: the decisive defeat is told in a single word
Nepos moves quickly away from Hannibal’s only great loss
the focus shifts at once to the feat of the retreat
it keeps the reader’s admiration for Hannibal

questions.q: how does Nepos make the retreat seem remarkable?
points: incredibile dictu: Nepos himself steps in to marvel
biduo et duabus noctibus: the exact, very short time
circiter milia passuum trecenta: the huge distance
the precise numbers make the claim sound measured and real
the focus moves from defeat to a feat of endurance
questions.guidance: Accept any three; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: where was Hadrumetum?
points: a coastal city south of Carthage (modern Sousse in Tunisia)

questions.lemma: quos non solum effugit, sed etiam ipsos oppressit
questions.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s response to the ambush impressive?
points: non solum … sed etiam builds to a climax
escape alone would have been enough
oppressit: he crushes his attackers too
ipsos: the very men who ambushed him

questions.q: what happened to Hannibal at Zama and in the days that followed?
points: a few days after the meeting he fought Scipio at Zama
he was beaten
he reached Hadrumetum in two days and two nights
a distance of about three hundred miles
the Numidians who had left the battle with him ambushed him
he escaped them
and crushed them
at Hadrumetum he gathered the survivors
within a few days, by fresh recruiting, he assembled a large army

questions.q: what impression of Hannibal does this give, and how?
points: his energy / resilience after a crushing defeat
contrast of paucis (few days) and multos (many men)
the chapter ends on contraxit, an image of rebuilding

questions.q: how does Nepos show the split between Hannibal and his city?
points: contrast: Hannibal prepares for war while his city makes peace
acerrime: the superlative stresses his energy
the peace is made behind his back

questions.q: what does this phrase suggest about Hannibal’s attitude to the peace?
points: he carried on regardless
as if the peace did not apply to him
he stayed in command of the army

questions.q: who was Mago?
points: Hannibal’s younger brother
he fought with Hannibal in Italy
he later commanded in Spain and northern Italy

questions.q: how did the Carthaginian envoys try to win Rome’s goodwill?
points: they came to Rome to thank the senate and people
for making peace with them
they presented a golden crown
the thanks and the gift come before any request

questions.q: how does Nepos make the senate’s refusal stand out?
points: gratum acceptumque: the reply opens graciously
the first request is granted (obsides … futuros)
the balance makes the refusal captivos non remissuros sharp
indirect speech gives the cool, formal tone of an official decree
questions.guidance: Accept any three; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: explain in your own words why the senate would not return the prisoners.
points: the Carthaginians still kept Hannibal
in command of an army
he was the man responsible for starting the war
he was Rome’s bitterest enemy
his brother Mago was also still in command

questions.q: why is this word important in the senate’s reply?
points: Rome’s complaint is that Hannibal is still in command
it shows Roman suspicion that the war is not really over while he holds an army
it puts pressure on Carthage to remove him

questions.q: why might Roman readers be startled by this phrase, and what was the office really?
points: rex (‘king’) was a hated word at Rome
the office was that of suffete
one of Carthage’s two chief magistrates
elected for a single year

questions.q: what did the envoys say and ask at Rome, and how did the senate reply?
points: they thanked the Romans for making peace
they presented a golden crown
they asked that their hostages be kept at Fregellae
they asked for their prisoners back
the senate said the gift was welcome and accepted
the hostages could stay where they asked
the prisoners would not be returned
because Hannibal was still in command of an army
and so was his brother Mago

questions.q: how does Nepos help his Roman readers understand Carthage’s government?
points: he compares the office with the Roman consulship
the balanced ut … sic sets the two cities side by side
annui bini: two each year, just like the consuls
Carthage is made to look like a mirror of Rome

questions.q: how does Nepos link Hannibal’s work in office with his career in war?
points: pari … ac: a comparison, so he shows exactly the same quality in peace as in war
diligentia: hard work / attention to detail, a quality Romans admired in a magistrate
it shows that his talents reach beyond the battlefield

questions.q: what does Nepos tell us about Hannibal’s time in office?
points: he showed the same energy / diligence
as he had shown in war
he raised new revenues
so that there was enough money
to pay what was owed to Rome under the treaty
there was also a surplus
which was stored in the treasury

questions.lemma: non solum ut esset pecunia … reponeretur
questions.q: how does Nepos emphasise the success of Hannibal’s reforms?
points: non solum … sed etiam builds to a climax: enough money, and then more besides
polyptoton esset … superesset: the step from enough to more than enough is heard in the words
in aerario reponeretur: there was money left over to store in the treasury
questions.guidance: Accept any two; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: explain in your own words why Hannibal decided to leave Carthage.
points: he believed the envoys had been sent
to demand that he be handed over (to Rome)
Nepos gives this as Hannibal’s own belief (ratus) and does not confirm it

questions.q: who was Antiochus?
points: Antiochus III (the Great), the Seleucid king who ruled a great empire from Syria
a king whose ambitions in Asia Minor and Greece brought him into conflict with Rome

questions.q: what did the Carthaginians do first when they learned of Hannibal’s flight?
points: when the flight became known
they sent two ships
to arrest him
if they could catch him

questions.q: how does Nepos make the Carthaginians’ treatment of Hannibal seem harsh?
points: asyndeton: the punishments follow one another with no connecting words, which sounds swift and relentless
bona eius publicarunt: all his property is taken
domum a fundamentis disiecerunt: his house is destroyed right down to its foundations
ipsum exulem: the list ends on Hannibal himself, declared an exile
the irony that the man who has just filled the treasury is punished by the city he served

questions.q: why do you think Nepos calls the Carthaginians by this name here?
points: Poeni is the usual Roman name for the Carthaginians / Phoenicians
Nepos switches to it just as the city turns on its own hero
it may suggest the treachery Romans associated with the Carthaginians, now aimed at Hannibal

questions.q: explain in your own words when and how Hannibal came back to Africa.
points: in the third year after he had fled his home
in the consulship of Lucius Cornelius and Quintus Minucius
with five ships
he reached Africa
in the territory of Cyrene

questions.q: what does this detail suggest about Hannibal’s situation?
points: it is a tiny force
it shows how far he has fallen from the commander of great armies
yet he still aims to drag Carthage into a war with Rome

questions.q: how does Nepos show that Hannibal still had influence over kings and states?
points: iam persuaserat: the pluperfect shows Antiochus had already been won over
spe fiduciaque: he works by persuasion, offering hope and confidence
he hopes to draw a whole state, Carthage, into the war (Carthaginienses … inducere)
cum exercitibus: the king agrees to send armies
in Italiam near the end: his goal is still Italy
questions.guidance: Accept any three; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: how does Nepos make the Carthaginians’ treatment of Mago seem unfair?
points: absentem: he is condemned while absent, without a hearing
eadem, qua fratrem: he is punished exactly like his brother, as though for belonging to the family
ubi … rescierunt: they act as soon as they find out, which seems hasty
the parallel treatment shows the whole city has turned against the Barca family

questions.q: how does Nepos convey the brothers’ plight as they set sail?
points: desperatis rebus: two words sum up how hopeless their situation was
alliteration of vela ventis gives weight to the phrase
vela ventis dedissent is a poetic phrase which suggests the brothers giving themselves up to fortune

questions.q: why do you think Nepos uses this word?
points: it is a diminutive, which sounds contemptuous (‘mere slaves’)
it makes Mago’s death a humiliating end for a famous commander
it contrasts sharply with the other version, death at sea

questions.q: what does this sentence suggest about Nepos’ opinion of Antiochus and of Hannibal?
points: Antiochus followed Hannibal’s advice in starting the war
he did not follow it in fighting the war
so Antiochus is to blame for the failure / acted foolishly
Hannibal’s advice would have carried the war to Italy, close to Rome
Hannibal is shown as the better strategist

questions.lemma: quem etsi … nulla deseruit in re
questions.q: what impression of Hannibal’s loyalty do we get, and how does Nepos create it?
points: Hannibal stays loyal even though the king acts foolishly
antithesis of multa stulte (many foolish schemes) and nulla … in re (not in a single matter)
stulte: a sharp criticism of the king, which makes Hannibal’s loyalty more striking
videbat: he saw the folly clearly and still stayed
etsi … tamen: the concessive structure stresses his loyalty in spite of everything

questions.q: what happened in Hannibal’s sea battle against Rhodes?
points: he commanded a few ships
which he had been ordered to bring
from Syria to Asia
with these he fought the Rhodian fleet
in the Pamphylian Sea
his side was beaten
by the enemy’s greater numbers
on the wing where he himself fought, he was victorious

questions.q: what happened to Antiochus at Thermopylae?
points: he was defeated by the Romans (in 191 BC)
after the defeat he withdrew to Asia

questions.q: explain in your own words what Hannibal feared at this point.
points: Antiochus had been defeated / put to flight
he was afraid that he would be handed over
to the Romans

questions.q: why do you think Nepos adds this comment?
points: it confirms that the danger was real
so Hannibal’s flight looks prudent / sensible
sine dubio: Nepos speaks in his own voice to assure the reader

questions.q: describe the danger Hannibal faced in Crete and the first part of his plan to deal with it.
points: he was in danger because of the greed of the Cretans
he was carrying a large sum of money
he knew word of it had got out
he filled several jars with lead
he covered the tops with gold and silver
he deposited them in the temple of Diana
in front of the leading citizens
pretending to entrust his fortune to their honesty

questions.q: how does Nepos make the trick clear and vivid?
points: historic presents complet, operit: we seem to watch Hannibal at work
antithesis of plumbo (worthless lead) and auro et argento (precious metals)
summas: only the tops are covered, so the whole deception is caught in a few words

questions.lemma: simulans se suas fortunas illorum fidei credere
questions.q: explain why this detail is ironic.
points: he pretends to trust their fides / honesty
the Cretans are known for their greed / dishonesty
the trick turns their own vice against them

questions.q: why would a temple be a natural place to leave money?
points: temples were often used as safe places to deposit money and valuables

questions.q: what impression of Hannibal’s cleverness do we get, and how does Nepos create it?
points: his in errorem inductis: the Cretans are fooled in a few words and the story moves straight on
omni sua pecunia: all his real money is hidden in the statues
in propatulo: the treasure lies in the open courtyard, in full view
abicit: ‘tosses aside’, so the real treasure seems carelessly left
quas secum portabat: statues he already had with him would raise no suspicion

questions.q: explain in your own words what the Gortynians were afraid of.
points: that Hannibal would remove his own property
without their knowledge
and take it away with him

questions.q: what does Nepos suggest about the Cretans here, and why does it matter for the story?
points: the Cretans are greedy
they had a proverbial reputation for greed and dishonesty
it explains why Hannibal’s money was at risk
the reader enjoys seeing the greedy outwitted

questions.q: who was Prusias, and where was his kingdom?
points: Prusias I, king of Bithynia
in north-west Asia Minor
on the coast of the Black Sea (which Nepos calls Pontus)

questions.q: how does Nepos neatly sum up the Cretan episode?
points: two ablative absolutes frame the subject Poenus
one sums up his money saved (conservatis suis rebus), the other the Cretans fooled (illusis Cretensibus)
omnibus: every single Cretan was fooled, which completes the joke
illusis: they have been made fools of

questions.q: how does Nepos show that Hannibal’s hatred of Rome had not changed?
points: eodem animo: the same attitude as ever, as Nepos promised in chapter 1
neque aliud quicquam egit: he did nothing else, which shows single-minded focus
armavit et exercuit: he arms and trains a king as if he were one of his soldiers
adversus Romanos comes last: the target is always Rome
erga Italiam: his thoughts are still on Italy

questions.q: explain in your own words what Hannibal noticed about Prusias.
points: the king’s own resources / the strength of his kingdom
were not enough for him to stand on his own / against his enemies
so he would need allies

questions.q: why do you think Eumenes is described in this way?
points: amicissimus: the superlative makes him Rome’s very close friend
he is defined by his friendship with Rome, the opposite of Hannibal
so the war against him becomes Hannibal’s war with Rome by proxy

questions.q: what do we learn about the war between Eumenes and Prusias?
points: it was already being fought
both on sea and on land
Eumenes was stronger on both fronts
because of his alliance with Rome

questions.q: how does Nepos show the ruthless logic of Hannibal’s thinking?
points: quo magis: Rome’s support for Eumenes only makes Hannibal more determined
opprimi: a violent verb, he wants Eumenes crushed
the condition si removisset shows clear strategic reasoning
faciliora … cetera: remove the key ally and everything else becomes easier

questions.lemma: ad hunc interficiundum talem iniit rationem
questions.q: how does Nepos lead the reader to expect another trick?
points: talem iniit rationem echoes capit tale consilium in the Cretan story
interficiundum: the gerundive states his aim bluntly: murder
the sentence ends looking forward to ‘the following plan’, so we wait to hear it

questions.q: what was about to happen?
points: within a few days the war would be decided / fought out at sea
a sea battle was coming

questions.q: explain in your own words why Hannibal had to fight by trickery.
points: he could not match the enemy in strength / weapons
so cunning / a stratagem was the only way to make up for this
he was outnumbered (in ships)

questions.q: why do you think Nepos mentions this detail?
points: the pots are cheap, ordinary clay
they would shatter when they landed
the homely detail makes the secret weapon all the more surprising
the pots hide what is inside them

questions.q: describe Hannibal’s preparations and the orders he gave his marines.
points: as many as possible
live venomous snakes
were to be collected
and put into earthenware pots
he collected a great number of them
on the very day of the sea battle
he called his marines together
all were to attack the one ship of King Eumenes
against the other ships they were only to defend themselves

questions.lemma: die ipso, quo facturus erat navale proelium
questions.q: why is the timing of Hannibal’s briefing important?
points: ipso: it was the very day of the battle
the plan was kept secret until the last moment
so the enemy could not learn of it
it raises the tension for the reader

questions.q: what further promise did Hannibal make to his men?
points: he would make sure they knew
which ship the king was sailing on

questions.q: what impression of Hannibal do we get, and how does Nepos create it?
points: he wants Eumenes out of the battle whatever it takes: aut cepissent aut interfecissent, either outcome will do
he knows how to motivate his men with a reward
hyperbaton of magno … praemio stresses the size of the reward
the chapter ends on the men’s incentive, so the reader expects a determined attack

questions.q: of which kingdom was Eumenes king?
points: Pergamum (in north-west Asia Minor)

questions.q: how does Nepos convey Hannibal’s confidence here?
points: facile: he tells his men they will manage it easily
serpentium multitudine: he trusts in the sheer number of snakes
indirect speech reports his orders briskly, as a commander sure of his plan

questions.q: what happened once Hannibal had encouraged his men?
points: the fleets of both sides
were led out
into battle

questions.q: explain in your own words what Hannibal did before the battle, and why.
points: once the battle lines were drawn up
before the signal for battle was given
he sent a messenger
in a small boat
carrying a herald’s staff
to show his own side
where Eumenes was

questions.q: how does this clause add to the tension?
points: it holds the fighting back
Hannibal’s trick takes place in the tense moment before the battle
the reader waits for the signal that has not yet been given
